Article Title: Spider-Man, Batman all had to pay rent: Magnus Carlsen, now a father, is no exception
Article Text:
Magnus Carlsen is now a father

Magnus Carlsen with his son

Magnus with his son

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

BENGALURU: Peter Parker still has to make rent. That's the part of the superhero myth that doesn't generally make it to the big screen.Spider-Man saves New York by night and shoots freelance photographs by day, not because he loves deadlines, but because somebody has to pay for groceries. Bruce Wayne funds the Batcave through a company he actually has to run. Even the billionaires among comic-book heroes tend to keep one foot planted in something as unglamorous as payroll, because the world they're protecting doesn't pause its bills just because they're busy saving it.The genius of that storytelling trope isn't the fighting. It's the quiet insistence that even extraordinary people don't get to opt out of ordinary responsibility. You can bend steel, but you still have to show up for the version of yourself that provides.It's a strange place to start a story about arguably the greatest chess player who has ever lived. But it's exactly where Magnus Carlsen 's own words landed, almost a year into fatherhood, when this journalist asked him what had actually changed since his son was born during a media interaction on the sidelines of the Global Chess League (GCL)."In my professional life, things haven't changed that dramatically," he replied almost instantly."I'm still the provider for the family, so I still work."Read that sentence twice. Here is a man who has spent two decades rewriting the ceiling of human chess ability, who has been declared unbeatable so many times that "unbeatable" started to feel like a job description rather than a compliment and the frame he reaches for, unprompted, to describe his life now is the oldest one in the book. Provider. Worker.The guy who still has to go to the office, except the office is a tournament hall on the other side of the world and the job is being the best that has ever done this.There's a reason that instinct runs so deep it shows up even in someone whose entire identity has otherwise been built on exceptionalism.Strip away the grandmaster titles and the rating numbers, and you're left with something Charles Darwin sketched out over a century and a half ago. In species where offspring depend heavily on parental care, one of the strongest pressures shaping behaviour is the survival and successful reproduction of the next generation.Natural selection doesn't reward talent, glory, or achievement for their own sake. It favours traits and behaviours that, on average, contribute to reproductive success. In a species where raising offspring is essential to that success, provisioning and protecting them can become an extraordinarily powerful behavioural priority.Every other instinct, ambition, or appetite can be renegotiated when that responsibility arrives. It's why the same species that produces reckless risk-takers also produces the most disciplined, repetitive, unglamorous labour imaginable, generation after generation, the instant there's a mouth to feed.Carlsen, without reaching for any of that language himself, described exactly this mechanism happening in real time inside his own life."Yeah, I love it (being a father)," he said, when asked how fatherhood had actually felt. "My son is the greatest human being alive. So, yeah, it's fantastic. It's a joy every day."Then, almost in the same breath, the other half of the equation. "It's a little bit sad to be away from him now, but I also have to provide for my family," he sighed.That sentence is the whole feature in miniature. Joy and duty, sitting right next to each other, unable to cancel each other out.It also explains something that had puzzled a lot of people watching Carlsen's career from the outside. Why would the greatest player alive walk away from the one title that carries his name to the widest audience, the classical World Championship, at the exact moment he could have kept collecting it?His own answer, delivered without a trace of nostalgia, sounded less like retirement and more like a man doing the math on his own limited hours."After I became a father as well, it made it even more certain for me that I was never coming back to the classical world championship," he told us, the reporters covering the GCL in Bengaluru.Not because he'd fallen out of love with chess.He was careful to draw that line clearly. "There are so many things that I like about chess. There are a lot of tournaments that I like. There are a lot of formats that I like," Magnus, currently plying his trade for defending champions APL Pipers, asserted.The classical world title specifically, though, had become something he "genuinely" disliked spending his finite time on, and once there was a small person at home whose future depended on how he spent his hours, "when there's no kind of competitive reason why I should, it makes zero sense."That's not the language of a man slowing down. It's the language of a man reallocating.Good enough, but when asked to reveal his son's name, the one detail every journalist in the room clearly wanted, Carlsen drew a boundary with the instinctive protectiveness of someone guarding something more fragile than a chess position."I can talk in general terms about my son. I think he's great, but I'm not sure I can do that," he said, gently declining. It's a small thing, a single guarded sentence in a room full of questions about tournaments and ratings. But it's also the most on-brand fatherhood answer imaginable.Somewhere between Darwin's finches and Peter Parker's rent money sits Magnus Carlsen, age 35, five-time world champion, currently building his entire professional calendar around a person the public isn't even allowed to know the name of. He didn't need evolutionary biology to explain why. He just needed one sentence. For him, it's a joy every day, and he still has to go to work because, you know, in a world where superheroes are not spared, not all superheroes wear capes.
Article Summary: Magnus Carlsen is now a father for the first time. The world's best chess player says he still has to work to provide for his family. "It's a little bit sad to be away from him now, but I also have to provide"

Article Title: 'Gukesh not in a position to defend anything': Magnus Carlsen on World Chess Championship clash vs Javokhir Sindarov
Article Text:
Magnus Carlsen on Gukesh vs Javokhir Sindarov World Championship clash

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

BENGALURU: Five-time world champion Magnus Carlsen has pushed back against the framing of D Gukesh's upcoming World Championship match as a "title defence", arguing that the Indian should instead be approaching it as an opportunity to gain rather than something to protect.Speaking to the reporters on the sidelines of the Global Chess League (GCL) on Thursday, Carlsen said the way Gukesh has played over the past two years means he shouldn't see himself as merely holding onto what he already has."The word 'defend' is really not a good place to begin, because in terms of how Gukesh has played for the last couple of years, he should not be in a position where he has to defend anything," Carlsen said. "He should be in a position where he has everything to gain."The Norwegian pointed to Gukesh's 2024 form as evidence of his ceiling."He has shown previously in 2024 that when things click, he has the potential to play at an extremely high level," Carlsen remarked, adding that while public confidence in a repeat performance may be low, that only sharpens the challenge in front of him. "I don't think a lot of people believe that he will do it now, but I think it's even more of an interesting challenge for him to try and get back to that."Carlsen was also blunt about the psychological dimension of the contest, suggesting the mental battle could prove just as decisive as anything on the board."Chess is a highly psychological game, so it probably won't take a lot to potentially place some doubts in Sindarov's mind and some confidence for Gukesh," he said.Asked whether Gukesh's current form would matter once the match got underway, Carlsen, who is currently playing for the APL Pipers in the fourth season of GCL, was candid about his broader scepticism of the classical World Championship format itself, calling it a poor mechanism for identifying the strongest player."One of the reasons why I believe it's an extraordinarily bad way to determine the best player in the world is that you play classical, which is the most egalitarian format, and you don't play a ton of games as well," he explained. Even a heavily lopsided pre-match assessment, he said, rarely translates into a lopsided scoreline."If you think a certain match is 80-20 before it starts, the likelihood is still very high that it's going to be a close score, because chess is such a drawish game."On the matchup itself, Carlsen was unequivocal that Gukesh holds his own against Sindarov in pure quality."Gukesh has shown that his ceiling is on par or better than Sindarov," he added. But given the short format, he warned that early momentum could decide everything."If Sindarov is ahead early on, it's probably very, very bad news for Gukesh. If Gukesh is ahead early on, he automatically becomes a significant favourite. That's how these matches work."
Article Summary: Five-time world champion Magnus Carlsen says D Gukesh should not see his upcoming World Championship match as a title defence. The Norwegian says the Indian should instead be approaching it as an opportunity to gain rather than something to protect. Carlsen was blunt about the psychological dimension of the contest, suggesting the mental battle could prove just as decisive as anything on the board.

Article Title: Elon Musk feels 'chess will be fully solved one day'; what does World No. 1 Magnus Carlsen think?
Article Text:
Elon Musk and Magnus Carlsen

What is his motivation behind coming to India for GCL?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Magnus Carlsen in Pipers dugout

BENGALURU: Elon Musk picked a fight with chess earlier this week. The world's richest man declared on X that chess will one day be "fully solved", the way checkers was cracked by computers back in 2007, with his logic being that most legal moves are so obviously bad that AI could eventually map the entire game.Chess.com's response was a masterclass in brevity. "Skill issue," they wrote. Musk doubled down anyway, insisting chess "is hard for humans, but not for computers" and would eventually be "fully solved like checkers" before admitting, almost sheepishly, that he'd spent his evening "arguing with some random intern" running the chess site's account.Chess.com wasn't about to let that slide. The person on the other end, it clarified, was in fact a full-time employee. The internet, predictably, had a field day.On Thursday, the current World No. 1 and five-time world champion Magnus Carlsen was asked about the emergence of AI in chess during an interview with the Indian media on the sidelines of the ongoing Global Chess League (GCL)."I'm not a computer expert, so I don't know if it's going to be solved," Carlsen, currently playing for the defending champions APL Pipers, shrugged.He did offer one technical correction, gently. Chess isn't unsolved so much as it's already "semi-solved" in the sense that matters most to players."We are pretty sure that it's a draw, and it's a draw in a tonne of ways. The margin is quite big", which is a rather more modest claim than Musk's vision of AI eventually calculating chess down to the last legal move."AI and computers in general have made the game a lot more accessible," he said. "You're now able to follow it, see the score, you're able to improve a lot faster."Asked what actually motivates him to keep showing up for a franchise-based league like GCL, he made the case for team chess with the same directness. "It's a really good format," he said. "I've said that from the start that we need team formats in chess that are genuinely exciting. The black-and-white format is very good."He wasn't shy about the parts he'd still tweak, pointing to the two-second increment added after move 40 as a concession to players he clearly has little patience for."I would have preferred for there not to be the two seconds after 40 moves as well," he explained. "That has been implemented on the request of players who are incompetent and lazy at times.""The format where you have the very clear white against black, matches are staggered, which is very good. The match is always going to be decisive unless there is a six-draw. I think there are a lot of good things about it."As for India specifically, Carlsen framed his regular return trips almost like a reset button. "I also like to come to India every second year or so because I need a year off to remind myself how crowded the tournaments are," he continued with a smile before adding warmly, "But parts of it I really enjoy. There's no atmosphere or enthusiasm like it in the east."
Article Summary: Magnus Carlsen says chess is already "semi-solved" in the sense that matters most to players. The world No. 1 was speaking on the sidelines of the Global Chess League (GCL) Carlsen: "AI and computers in general have made the game a lot more accessible"

Article Title: 'He shouldn't be here': Nasser Hussain bashes Pakistan with Virender Sehwag example
Article Text:
Saim Ayub and Virender Sehwag (Image credit: Agencies)

Hussain recalls Sehwag example

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Poll Vote & Share your view How crucial is match preparation for players transitioning from T20 to Test formats? Very crucial. Somewhat crucial. Not important. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Former England captain Nasser Hussain has slammed Pakistan’s decision to bring Saim Ayub into the Test team straight from the Caribbean Premier League (CPL), saying the young batter “shouldn't be here”.Ayub’s return to the Pakistan Test team ended in a nightmare as he was dismissed for a duck in both innings of the third Test against England at Edgbaston. The young opener faced only 11 balls across the two innings, with England pacer Ollie Robinson dismissing him on both occasions.Ayub had arrived in England after playing T20 cricket in the CPL. Hussain questioned why Pakistan chose to bring him into a Test match without enough preparation for the conditions.Speaking on Sky Sports after Pakistan finished Day 2 at 52-2 in their second innings, Hussain said Ayub should not have been picked for the Test.“The truth is he shouldn't be here. He came from the CPL and hasn't played first-class cricket in some time,” Hussain said during a post-day show on Sky Sports.Hussain said bringing a player directly from T20 cricket into a Test in England was a poor decision.“I don't know who thinks it's the right thing to fly someone over from foreign conditions, playing a completely different format, and think they're going to be fine in these conditions against a Dukes ball, against Ollie Robinson and England's bowling attack,” Hussain asserted, explaining why Ayub was destined to fail in these conditions against a team of the calibre of England.Hussain also recalled what happened when India once took a similar approach with Virender Sehwag Sehwag was flown into England without enough match practice and struggled at the same ground. Hussain said that if even a player of Sehwag’s experience could struggle, Pakistan should not have expected Ayub to immediately succeed.“Virender Sehwag tried it on this ground, if you remember... they flew him in. Virender Sehwag got a pair, and that's Virender Sehwag, who's a better, more experienced player than Saim,” highlighted Hussain.Hussain said Ayub must take some responsibility for the shot he played, but he questioned the decision-makers who selected him.“So a bit of responsibility goes to the lad for the shot he played. But also, whoever thought that was a seriously good decision and that he was going to go okay this week?”“It is just a sort of disrespect and disregard for Test match cricket. Test match cricket, as any cricketer will tell you, is the toughest format. Batting at the top of the order in England is the toughest task, and you just feel you can fly someone in from some part of the world and go, Good luck,” he said.
Article Summary: Saim Ayub was dismissed for a duck in both innings of the third Test against England at Edgbaston. The young opener faced only 11 balls across the two innings, with England pacer Ollie Robinson dismissing him on both occasions. Hussain questioned why Pakistan chose to bring him into a Test match without enough preparation for the conditions.

Article Title: 23 years after Rakesh Yadav, Tanya Chaudhary keeps Baghpat's hammer-throw legacy alive with national record
Article Text:
Tanya Chaudhary (TOI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: It took a minute for Tanya Chaudhary to put her feelings into words. She had very good reason to be overawed by the occasion. With a throw of 68.35m, the 22-year-old had just broken the national record in hammer throw at the Indian Athletics Series Final.Uttar Pradesh's Chaudhary had multiple aspects to celebrate at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium. She bettered Anushka Yadav's national record of 67.02m set in June. She had edged Anushka (66.34m) in the competition. The record comes within days of her flight to Japan for the Asian Games , which begin on August 19. Lastly, she had just put Baghpat back on the hammer throw map - something Rakesh Yadav had done with a 70.13m throw back in 2003.The 68.35m throw of the chain and iron was a big improvement on her personal best of 63.91m from last year. It was even higher than the 65.60m she had managed at the Inter-University Athletics Championships in January.Coached by Sachin Yadav, her foundations were set at the Shri Krishna Inter College in Baleni, Baghpat. And here, almost 70kms away, her goal of the past three years had been realised."I had been chasing this goal for the past three years. Earlier I had recorded 65m and I had registered it unofficially twice or thrice.But now that I've finally achieved that, and more, I am very pleased," she said with a smile.Her path to the Asian Games was not straightforward.Since January, she has struggled with injuries: a knee issue, a stress injury on the femur bone and an ACL. Then in June, under Bhubaneshwar's floodlights at the Inter-State Championships, she missed the qualification mark by mere two centimetres. Anushka, her UP compatriot, had topped the standings then while also registering the national record."I missed the national record the last time but it's a good thing that we (she and Anushka) come from the same training facility. So, it is a good thing for us to learn and compete with each," she told reporters after pocketing Rs 1 lakh as the winner of the event."That second place finish actually gave me a target, that it has even gotten bigger. That I need to put more effort, work on my shortcomings even more. It's a good thing that we have each other to compete with and improve upon," she continued.Despite the disappointment of missing the qualification mark straightaway, she still found her way into the 503-member Indian contingent for Aichi-Nagoya. The challenge there would be spearheaded by China's Jiale Zhang, who had set the continental record of 78.64m at the Chinese Championships."The target is to obviously do better. Now that I've improved on my personal best, the bare minimum would be to match it. The 70m goal is not far away now. It is now almost 1.5m away."My target this year was to achieve 70m but with injuries I was hampered and affected. But now that I've gained momentum, I am hopeful that I will be able to reach 70m also," she finished.
Article Summary: Uttar Pradesh's Chaudhary bettered Anushka Yadav's national record of 67.02m set in June. She had just put Baghpat back on the hammer throw map - something Rakesh Yadav had done with a 70.13m throw in 2003.

Article Title: 'Safeguarding is not just about harassment': Neetal Narang
Article Text:
Image credit: X

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: A confidential point of contact for athletes facing bullying, sexual or mental harassment, discrimination or isolation was unheard of at multi-disciplinary sporting events until a few years ago.That changed in 2022, when the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) made it mandatory for every contingent participating in events under its umbrella to appoint a safeguarding officer.At the 2025 Youth Asian Games , former shot-putter Om Prakash Karhana became the first person to take up the role for India. At the Asian Games, president of the Softball Association of India Neetal Narang will assume the responsibility.An IOC and OCA-certified safeguarding officer, Neetal has undergone several certification courses conducted by the continental body over the past two years. As an administrator, she believes the role is an important step towards creating a safe sporting environment.“We administrators exist only because of the athletes. They are the major stakeholders of the entire sporting ecosystem,” she told TOI.“I was always inclined to do something good for sportspeople because I’ve seen how vulnerable and fragile they become and sometimes feel helpless as well,” she added.For Neetal, safeguarding extends far beyond dealing with sexual harassment or bullying.“Safeguarding is not just about a few aspects like sexual harassment or bullying. We deal with a wider aspect of issues like physical, psychological and sexual abuse, harassment, neglect, discrimination and bullying. We tend to normalise or brush under the carpet issues like body shaming, which will also come under the safeguarding officer’s purview,” she explained.Being proactive, she believes, is crucial to the role.“It is important to be proactive, alert, aware and stay observant. You also have to be approachable, compassionate and inspire confidence in the athlete that what they speak is bound by confidentiality. The position comes with a huge amount of trust and responsibility,” she said.Gender sensitivity has also been a key part of Neetal’s training. Importantly, that includes creating a space where male athletes feel comfortable speaking about issues that affect them.“In our society, men are expected to stay strong at all times. That’s a notion we try to dispel and make them comfortable because men face a lot of tough situations and often struggle to open up about it,” she said.At the Asian Games, the organising committee, in collaboration with the OCA and participating nations, will set up safeguarding booths near the dining halls at various facilities. The athletes will also be provided with the contact details of the safeguarding officer for each contingent.Neetal’s first hands-on experience came at last year’s National Games in Uttarakhand, where she got an opportunity to put her training into practice.For the Asian Games, an outreach schedule has been prepared and athletes will attend an online session to familiarise themselves with the safeguarding mechanism and the support available to them.And when a complaint is raised, there is a defined escalation process.“We’ll have to escalate it to the Games Organising Committee and the OCA,” Neetal said.
Article Summary: Olympic Council of Asia made it mandatory for every contingent participating in events under its umbrella to appoint a safeguarding officer. Former shot-putter Om Prakash Karhana became the first person to take up the role for India at the 2025 Youth Asian Games. At the Asian Games, president of the Softball Association of India Neetal Narang will assume the responsibility.

Article Title: East Zone end 14-year wait, win Duleep Trophy for third time
Article Text:

CHENNAI: Fourteen years is a long wait. But when East Zone finally got their hands on the Duleep Trophy at the MA Chidambaram Stadium on Thursday, it felt less like a finish line and more like the culmination of a journey.The final, after all, had effectively been decided in the first two days. East piled up a staggering 708, South Zone were bowled out for 336 and a 372-run first-innings lead left little room for a comeback.East eventually declared at 388-7, sealing their third title as the final ended in a draw. Their previous triumph, in 2012-13, had also come at Chepauk.Skipper Ishan Kishan ensured East’s return to the top was memorable, smashing 270 in the first innings and 80 in the second, a combined 350 runs, the most by a batter in a Duleep final.“To be honest, it’s more about being one unit. We won this title as a group. Everyone was taking care of each other,” Kishan said after the match.There was plenty of promise beneath the experience. Teenager Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, the side’s vice-captain, had scored 92 in the semifinal while Kumar Kushagra hit a century in the final.Shikhar Mohan marked his Duleep Trophy debut with two fifties in the penultimate game. And then came Kounain Quraishi. In only his second firstclass game, the Shahbaz Ahmed replacement remained unbeaten on 116 on Day Five.Brief scores: East Zone 708 all out & 388-7 decl. (Quraishi 116*, Anukul 64). South Zone 336 all out.
Article Summary: East Zone beat South Zone to win the Duleep Trophy for the first time in 14 years. East piled up a staggering 708, South Zone were bowled out for 336. Ishan Kishan scored 270 in the first innings and 80 in the second.

Article Title: ‘Let me just play a little bit’: Geet Sethi makes billiards comeback at 65
Article Text:
Geet Sethi (Image credit: X)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

BENGALURU: He doesn’t look his age of 65, but Indian cuesports legend Geet Sethi is quick to acknowledge that appearances can be deceptive.“I may not look it, but I feel my age,” he laughs.But Sethi is like the classics — timeless.The ace cueist, who first picked up a cue in 1974, is set to return to competitive billiards next month, six years after his last appearance at the World Billiards Championship. The Ahmedabad-based cueist, who reached the knockouts at the 2018 edition, will return to the world stage in Great Wyrley, England, from Oct 19 to 22.Sethi’s comeback story began earlier this year when his peer and former cueist Ashok Shandilya coaxed him into playing a cuesports league in Dadar, Mumbai.“I played that tournament without really practicing. But it was so much fun. Then I came back home and said to myself, ‘Let me start. Let me just play a little bit,’” Sethi told TOI.Another spark was lit at the Sports Club of Gujarat in June.“The tournament was on the same lines as what I played earlier in Mumbai. Again, it was so much fun playing with music in the background and getting to meet the entire fraternity,” said the cuesports exponent-turned-seasoned entrepreneur.“It was so good to meet everybody collectively for a long period of time. Since then, I’ve been playing every day. I began to play decently enough to kind of start enjoying the game again. So that’s where the whole trigger started from,” added the nine-time world billiards champion.Before that tournament, Sethi had largely kept in touch with the sport by playing snooker occasionally. But it was a fellow member of the Sports Club of Gujarat who eventually nudged him towards the world championship.“A club member, who I play billiards with, kept pushing me. The thought really came when I started making breaks of 100 and 180. When you start enjoying the game, then the thought comes, I guess,” Sethi said.The opportunity to reconnect with old friends is another motivation.“I’m also going there just to meet up with all my old friends. In fact, the thought had come before to go just to go and meet up with everybody without playing.”Sethi admits he is excited rather than nervous about returning to the world arena.“I’m playing to a standard where at least I won’t make a fool of myself. There is no nervousness at all. I’m excited because even when you play the fun tournaments, it gets you into a lovely competitive mode, which is fabulous. It livens you up. So it’s more than nervousness. It’s exciting to feel the adrenaline kick again,” he said.As for what lies ahead, Sethi is keeping it simple.“I’m 65. I’ll take it one tournament at a time.”
Article Summary: Geet Sethi set to return to competitive billiards six years after his last appearance. Ahmedabad-based cueist will return to the world stage in Great Wyrley, England, from Oct 19 to 22. Sethi first picked up a cue in 1974 and is a nine-time world champion.

Article Title: ‘No parent is comfortable’: K Humpy pinpoints hurdle holding girls back in chess
Article Text:
Indian chess grandmaster Koneru Humpy (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Bengaluru: K Humpy, India’s first-ever woman chess player to attain a Grandmaster title, has witnessed dramatic changes to the landscape of the cerebral sport over the last 30-odd years.“Chess was not a commercial sport and women’s chess was not at all (commercial). So even after I became a GM, after being women’s world No. 2 for many years, there was not much money involved in the sport. When I won the Grand Prix, I think my prize money was about 6,000 euros,” said 39-year-old Humpy after her team Alpine APL Pipers, led by Magnus Carlsen on the top board, defeated Mumba Masters 11-6 in the Global Chess League (GCL) on Wednesday.“Now, you have Cairns Cup and Norway Chess, where the first prize for women is about 60,000 euros. The Tata Steel Rapid & Blitz event in India also gives equal prize to women, plus starting fees (appearance money). Sport is becoming more commercial. So, if you have the talent, you can sustain professionally.”Still, very few U-15 girls the world over belong to the Elo 2000 rating bracket, only about 60 compared to 850 boys.Asked what is stopping the vast majority of girls who shine at the age-group girls’ events but remain far off from the GM title, Humpy said: “The major difference is that the parents give more freedom to boys to go to any chess club or to someone’s house. So, they’ll sit with other boys and male players and start working. But when it comes to teenage girls, no parent is comfortable sending a girl alone.“If we have regular training camps where the girls will come and attend along with other boys and with some International Masters or GMs, they’ll definitely pick up fast. I don’t know who can do it, state body, (national) federation or maybe some private parties,” Humpy said.Results (Day 5): APL Pipers 11 bt Mumba Masters 6, Triveni Kings 3 lost to Ganges Grandmasters 15, Mumba 6 lost to Alaskan Knights 11, American Gambits 8 bt Triveni 5.
Article Summary: Koneru Humpy is India’s first-ever woman chess player to attain a Grandmaster title. Alpine APL Pipers, led by Magnus Carlsen on the top board, defeated Mumba Masters 11-6 in the Global Chess League.

South Zone's Tilak Varma (PTI Photo)

Chennai: Tilak Varma was finally dismissed in this year’s Duleep Trophy, falling agonisingly short of a second century. Despite being dismissed for 99, the South Zone captain’s red-ball ambitions stay intact, even though his team is staring at a big loss against East at the MA Chidambaram Stadium.Tilak, who had scored a century and a half-century in South Zone’s semifinal win against North Zone without being dismissed, battled through the Chennai heat on Wednesday against a quality East Zone attack. He was the last man to fall, giving a return catch to off-spinner Kounain Quraishi, as South were eventually bowled out for 336, conceding a massive 372-run first-innings lead.East, opting to bat again rather than send their bowlers back out, were 212-5 at stumps on Day Four, stretching their lead to 584.For Tilak, however, the larger picture remained clear. The 23-year-old left-hander has made no secret about his desire to play Test cricket for India.“I always say to everyone that I want to play red-ball cricket for India, that’s my biggest goal. As a kid, I thought I would play Test cricket first and then white-ball cricket. Red-ball cricket has always been my favourite, it’s my ‘A’ game,” Tilak said.“Over the last five-six years, I have played a lot of white-ball cricket and become good at it.Red-ball cricket is still my favourite, but I am comfortable with both now,” said Tilak.Tilak resumed the day on 56 and immediately took the attack to Mohammed Shami (2-42), striking two boundaries in the opening over. He and Chama Milind took 44 runs from the nine overs of Shami and Mukesh Kumar’s (3-62) combined first spell, putting them under pressure.Shami conceded 25 in his first four overs after giving away only 17 in 11 overs on Day 3.Kishan breaks 16-year-old recordEast’s second innings saw Ishan Kishan continue his first-innings form with 80 off 98 balls, while Shikhar Mohan (52) also remained among the runs.Ishan Kishan amassed 350 runs across both innings of the Duleep Trophy final, surpassing Dinesh Karthik’s aggregate of 333 runs from the 2010 final to set a new record for the most runs in the tournament final.Brief scores: East Zone 708 & 212-5 (I Kishan 80, S Mohan 52; Md Siraj 1-17) vs South Zone 336 (T Varma 99; M Kumar 3-62, Md Shami 2-42, M Quraishi 2-99).
Article Summary: South Zone captain Tilak Varma finally dismissed in Duleep Trophy final. South bowled out for 336, conceding 372-run first-innings lead to East. East opting to bat again rather than send bowlers back out, were 212-5 at stumps.

NEW DELHI: The T20I team had its first practice session at the Ferozeshah Kotla on Thursday afternoon ahead of the three-match series against Afghanistan starting on Sunday.After months of rehab at the Centre of Excellence (CoE), Jasprit Bumrah and Nitish Kumar Reddy were declared fit to join the team which will fly to Japan for the Asian Games two days after the series.Also on Thursday morning, the Indian cricket board (BCCI) announced that Harshit Rana had suffered another injury during his match simulation test at the CoE on Tuesday. Pacer Yash Thakur was named as his replacement.The recurring injuries have become a roadblock for the team management and selection committee as they try to firm up the preparation for next year’s ODI World Cup in southern Africa.It has emerged that the Indian cricket board (BCCI) has decided to let go of Team India physio Kamlesh Jain in the wake of frequent injuries. TOI had reported on Aug 6 that BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia had pulled up Jain for the spate of injuries to top players.The depth in Indian cricket allows India to make multiple T20I teams. It’s the ODI format that has become a headache for the team management.There has been some disagreement in BCCI circles about sending a full-strength T20I team for the Asiad while there are ODIs lined up against West Indies.Even as Abhishek Sharma and Sanju Samson went through their batting sessions in the practice area, head coach Gautam Gambhir was seen spending more time with T20I captain Shreyas Iyer and Washington Sundar — two integral members of the ODI team — when they were batting at the centre square.When the ODI series against West Indies starts in Thiruvananthapuram on Sept 27, Gambhir will be without first-choice ODI players like Bumrah, Iyer, Washington, Axar Patel, Ishan Kishan and Reddy.There’s no clarity about when allrounder Hardik Pandya will be available even as he undergoes an unending rehab at the CoE.While the World Cup may seem a year away, the number of ODIs are few and far between. It has left very little breathing space for the team management and the selectors to firm up the ODI core team.Meanwhile, India’s fast bowling coach Morne Morkel hasn’t yet joined the team. Sources said he is yet to receive his visa renewal.The Delhi and District Cricket Association (DDCA) said that the first T20I on Sept 13 will go ahead as scheduled even as the Delhi traffic police wrote a letter to the association requesting to move the match in light of the BRICS summit.In a letter, the DCP (traffic) said the summit would require extensive traffic arrangements, including VVIP/VIP route regulation and deployment of personnel.However, DDCA later posted on X saying the match was on.“The 1st T20I will go ahead as scheduled. Following a meeting with Delhi traffic police, DDCA has been assured of all support,” the association said.
Article Summary: First T20I to go ahead despite traffic police request to reschedule match. Jasprit Bumrah and Nitish Kumar Reddy declared fit to join the team. Harshit Rana suffered another injury during his match simulation test.

Article Title: Shafali stars with 64, Deepti strikes thrice as India storm into 10th Asia Cup final after 40-run win over Bangladesh

Deepti spins Bangladesh into trouble

India eye another Asia Cup title

India produced another dominant performance with bat and ball to beat Bangladesh by 40 runs and storm into the final of the Women’s Asia Cup 2026 at the Dubai International Cricket Stadium on Thursday. After posting 149/6 in their 20 overs, India’s bowlers delivered under pressure to restrict Bangladesh to 109/7, successfully defending what initially appeared to be a modest total on a slow pitch.The victory extended India’s unbeaten run in the tournament and secured their place in a 10th successive Women’s Asia Cup final. They will face the winner of the second semi-final between defending champions Sri Lanka and Pakistan in the title clash on September 13.Bangladesh won the toss and opted to field, but Shafali Varma made the most of the opportunity to put India on the front foot.The explosive opener smashed 64 off 40 balls, hitting seven fours and three sixes, as she held India’s innings together after vice-captain Smriti Mandhana fell for just two. Shafali rode her luck after being dropped three times but made Bangladesh pay with an attacking knock that gave India a competitive total.Captain Harmanpreet Kaur struggled for fluency but contributed 24 off 28 balls, including two sixes, while Richa Ghosh added an important 21 off 16 deliveries. Deepti Sharma then provided the late impetus with a quick 13 off six balls, helping India finish just short of 150.Bangladesh needed 150 to reach the final but struggled to maintain momentum throughout their chase. Deepti Sharma once again proved the difference with the ball, claiming 3/26 in four overs and repeatedly breaking Bangladesh's resistance.Nandani Sharma also impressed, taking 2/10 from two overs, including the final wicket of the innings. Bangladesh’s top order showed glimpses of resistance, with Dilara Akter scoring 21 off 26 balls and Shorna Akter hitting a brisk 22 off 18. But the batting line-up failed to absorb India's sustained pressure.The Tigresses lost wickets at regular intervals as India tightened their grip on the chase. With the required rate climbing, Bangladesh could only reach 109/7 in 20 overs, falling 40 runs short.The innings ended in fitting fashion for India, with Nandani Sharma dismissing Rabeya Khan hit-wicket. Khan attempted to slog a slower delivery but ended up dislodging the stumps with her bat while completing the shot.India’s latest victory keeps their unbeaten campaign intact and sends them into yet another Asia Cup final. The seven-time champions will now await the winner of Sri Lanka vs Pakistan, with the final scheduled for September 13.
Article Summary: India beat Bangladesh by 40 runs in Women's Asia Cup 2026 semi-final. Shafali Varma hit 64 off 40 balls, hitting seven fours and three sixes. Deepti Sharma took 3/26 in four overs and Nandani Sharma took 2/10. India will face the winner of Sri Lanka vs Pakistan in the final on September 13.

England strengthened their grip on the third Test against Pakistan at Edgbaston on Thursday, piling up 453 in their first innings before reducing the visitors to 52/2 at stumps on Day 2.Having started the day with a 23-run lead, England added another 297 runs across the first two sessions to take a massive 320-run first-innings lead. Pakistan then endured a nightmare start to their second innings, losing both openers in Ollie Robinson’s opening over.Shan Masood and Azan Awais offered some resistance before rain and bad light brought an early end to play. Pakistan still trail by 268 runs, with eight wickets in hand.Resuming on 156/4, England’s middle and lower order kept Pakistan’s bowlers under pressure throughout the morning and afternoon sessions. Harry Brook top-scored with 75, while Jamie Smith made 69 and Dan Lawrence contributed 65. Emilio Gay also struck a fluent 60 before Ollie Robinson added a rapid 50 off 47 balls.Five England batters passed fifty, but none could convert their starts into a century. The hosts were eventually bowled out for 453 shortly before tea.Pakistan debutant Razaullah was their most successful bowler, finishing with 4/148. He had moments of promise but struggled to contain England’s scoring rate, while Mohammad Ali and Mohammad Imran picked up two wickets each.Pakistan needed a strong response after being asked to bat again with a 320-run deficit, but Robinson immediately exposed their top order. The England seamer removed Saim Ayub for a first-ball duck before dismissing Abdullah Shafique soon after, leaving Pakistan 0/2.Robinson, who has been England’s standout bowler in the series, finished the day with 2/10 and once again gave Pakistan’s batters plenty to think about.With Pakistan in serious trouble, captain Shan Masood and Azan Awais steadied the innings with an unbeaten 52-run partnership for the third wicket. Masood was unbeaten on 21, while Awais made 29 not out when rain interrupted play.The weather eventually forced an early finish, with the ground staff unable to prepare the outfield in time for a restart.At 52/2, Pakistan remain 268 runs behind England and have yet to cross the 200-run mark in any of their innings in this three-Test series. England, meanwhile, are firmly in control and will sense an opportunity to complete a 3-0 series sweep.
Article Summary: England bowled Pakistan out for 453 on Day 2 of third Test at Edgbaston. Ollie Robinson took two early wickets to put Pakistan in trouble. Pakistan still trail by 268 runs, with eight wickets in hand. Harry Brook top-scored with 75, while Jamie Smith made 69 and Dan Lawrence contributed 65.

From a village in Tripura to Commonwealth Games glory

CM urges Asmita to target Asian Games success

NEW DELHI: Tripura chief minister Manik Saha has fulfilled a promise made to Commonwealth Games gold medallist Asmita Dey, with the state government allotting her a piece of land in Agartala to build a house.The 23-year-old judoka was honoured in Tripura on Wednesday after becoming the first Indian judoka to win a Commonwealth Games gold medal.Dey won the women’s -48kg title in Glasgow after defeating Canada’s Heidi Quach in a dramatic golden-score contest. The state government also presented her with a cheque of Rs 10 lakh as part of the felicitation.Speaking at the event, Saha highlighted Dey’s difficult journey from a small village in South Tripura to the top of the Commonwealth Games podium. Her father, he noted, worked as a cycle mechanic in Sonaichari.“The journey from an obscure village in South Tripura to a podium finish at Glasgow was a race against time. Her father was a cycle mechanic at Sonaichari. Against all odds, she stood firm on her mission and achieved phenomenal success for the country,” he said.The chief minister recalled meeting Dey at Tripura Bhavan in New Delhi after her return from the Games.During that meeting, the judoka had expressed her wish to have a house in Agartala.“During the meeting, Asmita revealed she desperately wanted a house in Agartala. I promised to fulfil her wish, and today a piece of land has been allotted to her,” he said.Saha said Dey’s achievement could motivate more young athletes from Tripura to pursue sport at the highest level. He also urged her to remain disciplined as she prepares for the Asian Games, particularly because of the strict anti-doping requirements.“I urge Asmita to remain alert, particularly about food, because she has to pass through a stringent dope test before joining the prestigious Asian Games. We believe she will shine again in the Asian Games by winning a medal for the country,” he said.Youth Affairs and Sports Minister Tinku Roy, Agartala Mayor Dipak Majumder and Arjuna award-winning gymnast Dipa Karmakar were among those who attended the felicitation ceremony.
Article Summary: Tripura chief minister Manik Saha has fulfilled a promise made to Commonwealth Games gold medallist Asmita Dey. The state government allotting her a piece of land in Agartala to build a house. Article Title: Rajasthan stuck in 2012, Manipur in 2023: How actively are states with CWG medals promoting sports?
Article Text:
Are sports bodies of Indian states promoting the game properly?

Medal tally of India's athletes by birth state/UT

Haryana: Hit on the podium, not so much off it

Manipur still talking about 2023

Rajasthan: 14 years and counting

Uttar Pradesh and Delhi carry the same gloomy picture

And then come Tamil Nadu and others

The ones somewhere in the middle

How active are states/UTs with CWG medallists in promoting sport

Does it matter so much?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is more important for grassroots sports promotion? Social media presence Local sports events Government funding 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: Somewhere on a muddy school field in Haryana right now, a teenager is perhaps drilling the same throwing technique over and over, just as she had watched on television just days ago. Her sole aim is to pull off the one like Sharmila Dhankar, India's Commonwealth Games shot put gold medallist.Before the 2026 CWG campaign, she, like many of us, had almost certainly never heard the name. And it's not because Dhankar had not won anything before the Glasgow Games; she had, a gold medal in the Women's Shot Put F57 event at the 2026 Fazza International Para Athletics Championship, but because one of the primary institutions whose entire job was to carry that story back from the medal podium to villages and training grounds across the state has, for all practical purposes, gone quiet.That's the part of this story that rarely gets told. India walked away from Glasgow with 39 medals, and for a week, the athletes who won them were everywhere, garlanded at airports, seated beside ministers, their faces on the evening news. But medals don't build the next generation of athletes by themselves. Somebody has to keep telling their stories, long after the felicitation photo is filed away, to the kid training in a dusty school ground who needs proof that this path actually leads somewhere.We wanted to know which state sports departments are still doing their job of promoting the sports and their grassroots on their social media platforms, and which ones seem to have simply logged off. So we scrolled through the timelines ourselves. Here's what we found.No state produced more glory in Glasgow than Haryana. Eleven medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze, spanning boxing, wrestling, athletics, and para sport, headlined by a Neeraj Chopra silver that will be replayed on sports channels for years.Alongside him were names most of India still had little knowledge of. The likes of Preeti Pawar, Jaismine Lamboria, Sakshi Chaudhary, Priya Ghanghas, Sachin Siwach, and Ankush Panghal, all of whom trained in government facilities, under government schemes, and who'd probably appreciate their own state department cheering as loudly for them as it does for its concert lineups.Because that's the thing. The Sports Department, Government of Haryana's X account has posted exactly once in all of 2026, and it's a flyer for the music acts playing at the Chief Minister's Cup.Facebook and Instagram follow a similar rhythm with a short cluster of posts around that February event, and then not much else.Eleven medals, and not one dedicated post to show for it. Somewhere in Rohtak or Bhiwani, a young pugilist training in Priya Ghanghas's discipline would probably just like a little proof that someone up top is paying attention.Manipur's page has an odd time-capsule quality to it. This is the state that gave India Mirabai Chanu, one of the country's most beloved Olympic medalists, and this Commonwealth Games alone produced four medalists from Manipur, Chanu's gold among them, alongside Rishikanta Singh, Bindyarani Devi, and Jadumani Singh.And yet the Department of Youth Affairs & Sports' X account hasn't posted since October 2023, a "Run for Unity" event, frozen well before any of this year's medals happened.Although the Facebook page has had a few sporadic posts here and there this year, its Instagram account has managed just two posts since January. It’s the kind of gap that makes you wonder if someone simply forgot the login details somewhere along the way.If there's one number in this whole exercise worth sitting with, it's this: the official Sports Department, Government of Rajasthan hasn't posted on Facebook since April 14, 2012.Fourteen years, through Arundhati Choudhary's Commonwealth gold and everything else that's happened in Rajasthan sport since.Its X account's last original post predates a retweet from March 2021, and there's no Instagram at all. A parallel handle, the Rajasthan State Sports Council, exists across all three platforms and is barely livelier.Somewhere behind Choudhary's medal is a genuinely good story, but it just hasn't found a home on the one page built to tell it.Gulveer Singh managed both a silver and a bronze for Uttar Pradesh this Games, a rare double that would make a great centrepiece for the state's sporting year. Instead, across two separate official handles on three platforms, Uttar Pradesh Sports has produced little beyond reposts, while its sister account, Sports Directorate, Govt of Uttar Pradesh, hasn't posted at all in 2026.Delhi Government, for its part, doesn't run a dedicated sports account at all on any of the popular social media platforms, so gold medalist Harsh Singh and bronze medalist Tejaswin Shankar, both representing India's capital, don't really have an institutional cheerleader online, their wins quietly absorbed into the general churn of city government updates. Both athletes are, in effect, doing their own promotional legwork.Set against all that quiet, Tamil Nadu feels like a different sport altogether. Its Sports Tamil Nadu handles post multiple times a day, celebrating not just its own three medalists, Praveen Chithravel, Selva Prabhu, Muthupandi Raja, but athletes from other states too, weaving in government scheme updates without it ever reading like bureaucracy.Every medallist got a dedicated post. Somewhere in Tamil Nadu, a kid training in long jump or wrestling doesn't have to wonder whether the sport leads anywhere. The state tells them, publicly, almost daily.Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka's Facebook and Instagram pages, Assam, Bihar, and Tripura all follow a version of that same habit, active, consistent, generous with attention toward athletes nobody outside their district would otherwise know existed.Kerala doesn't run a separate sports handle on X but keeps its Facebook and Instagram genuinely lively, making sure Murali Sreeshankar and Mohammed Basil's silvers got their due.Andhra Pradesh mirrors that same rhythm across all three platforms.Not every state falls neatly into being inactive or staying proactive. Punjab's account managed just two posts on X all year, New Year's and Republic Day, though its Facebook and Instagram carry a bit more life around coaching and departmental meetings, even if athletes rarely get top billing.Uttarakhand was genuinely active last year before cooling off in 2026, leaning more toward government scheme announcements on Facebook, though its Instagram at least carried two posts around the Games.Maharashtra has dedicated posts up for both Sarvesh Kushare and Dilip Gavit, with Instagram staying fairly regular, enough effort to stay out of the quiet column.Karnataka's X account hasn't posted since March 2024, around an unrelated cultural-team event, even though its Facebook and Instagram have stayed warm and active toward its CWG medalists.It is worth asking why this actually matters, beyond good manners. Well, a state sports department's social media feed isn't just a courtesy board for congratulations; it's one of the cheapest, most direct tools available to build the next generation of athletes.A youngster in a small town is far more likely to pick up a javelin because they saw a state government post celebrating someone from their own district. Even when it comes to promoting any government policy, social media can be as effective.Visibility drives aspiration. There's a funding logic too. Sponsors, corporates, and even state finance departments allocate resources partly based on visible public interest, and a well-run social account is often the easiest evidence a sport has that interest.ALSO READ: Anahat Singh: What is in the name? A word from Guru Nanak's prayer, now India's squash sensation Silence, on the other hand, sends the message that grassroots sport isn't a priority worth the effort of a single post, even when the state has just produced a medallist on the world stage.It is worth it because sometimes, the first step towards building a sporting culture is simply showing people that their achievements are being seen.
Article Summary: India won 39 medals at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Haryana produced 11 medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze. But the state sports department has posted just once in all of 2026. What do you think is more important for grassroots sports promotion? Government funding or social media presence? Share your view.

Article Title: ‘That video was not ordinary’: PM Modi praises Lovlina for objecting to distorted India map - Watch
Article Text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi shares a light moment with boxer Lovlina Borgohain. (PTI Photo)

‘That video was not ordinary’

Mirabai opens up about four difficult years

Narender's joke leaves Modi laughing

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Boxer Lovlina Borgohain's decision to object to a distorted Indian map during the Commonwealth Games earned special appreciation from Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time.Lovlina, who won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow, was among India's medal winners who interacted with Modi at his residence on Sunday. The meeting, attended by Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya, Minister of State for Sports Raksha Khadse and Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha, saw athletes recount their experiences from the Games in an informal and emotional setting.In a little over 10-minute video of the interaction shared by the Prime Minister's Office on Monday, Modi brought up Lovlina's confrontation with a restaurant in Glasgow after she noticed a distorted Indian map.“Kya hua wo restaurant waale se jhagda kar rahi thi? (What happened, you were fighting with that restaurant guy?)” Modi asked.Lovlina laughed before explaining why she intervened.“We had such a good performance and it was the last day of the Games. It was a happy occasion sir, we were celebrating and I didn't like it when I saw the distorted map. I politely told them and they have made the changes also,” she explained.Modi applauded the boxer for noticing the issue despite being in the middle of celebrations after her medal-winning campaign.“To be able to recognise the significance of that map at a time when you were celebrating and the Games were over, I can tell you truthfully, that video was not ordinary. It will be remembered by people for a very long time,” he told the Tokyo Olympics bronze medallist.India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.The interaction also provided an emotional window into Mirabai Chanu's journey to her gold medal in the women's 48kg category. The weightlifter produced a Games-record lift of 190kg, but her triumph came after four difficult years following her one-kilogram miss at the Paris Olympics. Modi asked Mirabai about the tears she shed on the podium and even fed her a laddu during their interaction.“Itne aansu tapak rahe the (So many tears were rolling down),” Modi remarked.Mirabai explained that the tears represented years of accumulated emotions.“I was very happy and emotional at that moment. I was crying because I missed a medal in the Paris Olympics by one kilogram. I have faced a lot in these last four years. I was battling injuries and some family problems too.“There were a lot of things. So, these four years were very tough for me. And when I stood on the podium, our flag went up and the anthem played, it was hard to stop myself,” she said.The meeting also had its lighter moments. Boxer Narender Berwal, who won silver in the +90kg category, recalled a funny exchange with a Pakistani boxer after beating him at the 2015 World Military Games.“During the 2015 World Military Games, I had a bout with a Pakistani boxer. I won it but when we were together in the medical room for treatment to our niggles, he said to me 'Bhaijan aapka naam Narender hai, aapke coach ka naam Narender hai, aapke Pradhan Mantri ka naam Narender hai, mujhe Narender naam se nafrat ho gayi hai.' (Brother, you, your coach and your PM are all named Narender. I hate this name now),” he recalled, drawing laughter from Modi.The Prime Minister also underlined the broader significance of the athletes' achievements, saying their medals were helping inspire a new generation.“I have been in this house for 12-13 years now and if there is one group that I have met regularly here, it is the athletes because of your efforts to win medals for India and your tradition of scaling new heights.“Far more than our push to promote sports in schools, it is your medals that inspire people,” Modi said.
Article Summary: Lovlina Borgohain won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow. Prime Minister Narendra Modi described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time. India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.

Article Title: ‘From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping’: PM Modi’s heartfelt message to CWG heroes - Watch

NEW DELHI: “From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping.”Prime Minister Narendra Modi had an emotional message for Mirabai Chanu as he interacted with India's Commonwealth Games 2026 medal winners at his residence on Sunday, reflecting on the sacrifices behind the country's successful campaign in Glasgow.Modi hosted the medal-winning contingent at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg and heard athletes recount some of the moments that defined their journeys at the Games. I feel as if from every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping,” Modi told the Olympic silver medallist.Mirabai, who won gold in Glasgow, opened up about the difficult journey that preceded her Commonwealth Games triumph, including the disappointment of the Paris Olympics.“I was very happy, and emotional too. That day the happiness was greater and I cried because at the Paris Olympics, I lost a medal by 1 kg. In a player’s life what all we have to face. So within these 4 years, how much and what all I had faced, every time injuries were going on and all that was happening.So with great difficulty I had faced these 4 years. So when all that happened, on the podium when I stood, sir, and when our flag goes up and our national anthem plays, sir, we cannot stop, sir, tears come out on their own,” she said.Modi responded by highlighting the wider impact of the athletes' achievements.“This is very good. It is not as if this achievement of yours is considered only your achievement; your victory becomes a very big inspiration for the coming generations.”The informal interaction also saw athletes share lighter and deeply personal moments from their Glasgow campaigns.Modi reminded para shot put gold medallist Sharmila Dhankar of a promise she had made earlier.“You made a promise. Last time, yours, both daughters will become players,” Modi said with a smile.Dhankar replied: “Haanji, right now they are young in age. In the next Commonwealth, one family will bring 3 medals.”Men's 100m T47 gold medallist Dilip Gavit, meanwhile, spoke about dedicating his performance to his guru.“When I was running, when my event was on 29th (July), that day was Guru Purnima, so that day I gave a gift to my guru,” he was heard saying in the video.In another video posted by Modi, gold medallist boxer Sakshi Chaudhary introduced herself and the contingent.“Hello friends! This is Sakshi Chaudhary. Today, our honourable Prime Minister has invited us, the Commonwealth Games medalists, and we feel very proud. We are extremely happy to have met him; he is very humble. Sir, would you like to say something?” she said.Modi replied with a message that summed up his interaction with the athletes: “Jo khelega, woh khilega” (The one who plays, will blossom). “Always cheer for Bharat.”India's fourth-place finish came despite a significantly smaller contingent and a reduced sporting programme compared to Birmingham 2022. Article Title: From hospital bed to CWG gold: How Jaismine Lamboria fought the odds in Glasgow
Article Text:
India's Jaismine Lamboria celebrates after winning the women's 57kg boxing final. (AP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Just weeks before stepping into the ring at the Commonwealth Games, Jaismine Lamboria wasn’t thinking about medals. She was searching for answers. The recurring fever had refused to go away.Multiple medical tests showed nothing unusual and the Indian boxer tried to push through, managing the symptoms with paracetamol. When the illness persisted, she was admitted to a hospital in Mohali. Doctors finally diagnosed a bacterial infection, putting her on an intensive 14-day course of medication. For an athlete preparing for one of the biggest competitions of the year, it could easily have been the end of the campaign.Instead, it became the beginning of one of the most remarkable comebacks of her career. “I was avoiding further medical tests because the initial reports were coming back normal. We didn’t know what exactly had to be treated. Finally, after I was admitted, they detected a bacterial infection and I was on medication for 14 days,” the 57kg boxer said.When she was discharged, the clock was already ticking. Barely three weeks remained before the Games.“I started training only on July 1. Initially it was just warm-up, walking and stretching. I had very little time, so we had to be patient.”The physical recovery was only one part of the challenge. During those uncertain weeks, sports psychologist Priya Vrinda became a constant source of support, ensuring the illness didn’t break her confidence.“When I was sick, I was already connected with Priya Vrinda ma’am. She kept me mentally strong and never allowed me to go down,” Jaismine said. That resilience was evident when she returned to competition. Jaismine boxed with maturity, tactical discipline and composure to upgrade the Commonwealth bronze she had won four years ago into gold in the 57kg.One of Jaismine’s biggest assets inside the ring has been her reach in her category. While every opponent may not be shorter — Jaismine stands five feet seven inches in her socks — she believes her physical advantage has become an important weapon thanks to careful coaching. “My coaches taught me how to use my reach properly. It definitely gives me an advantage in many bouts.”
Article Summary: Jaismine Lamboria won gold in the women's 57kg boxing at the Commonwealth Games. The Indian boxer had been suffering from a recurring fever. Doctors diagnosed a bacterial infection and put her on a 14-day course of medication. Jaismine credits her coach Priya Vrinda with helping her recover.

Article Title: How Jadumani Singh's risky weight change nearly derailed his CWG dream before winning Glasgow silver
Article Text:
India's Jadumani Singh Mandengbam (PTI Photo)

A bold gamble after the 50kg category disappeared

The selection maze before Glasgow

Jadumani Si​ngh's Road to CWG Silver (AI-generated Infographic)

The Sports Ministry hurdle

Jadumani Singh Mandengbam (PTI Photo)

Why the gold slipped away

File Pic: L Sarita Devi (PTI Photo)

Olympic gold remains the ultimate dream

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: When Indian pugilist Jadumani Singh Mandengbam stepped onto the podium to receive the men's 55kg silver medal at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, it marked the culmination of a journey that had almost ended before it had even begun.The 22-year-old Manipuri boxer was one of India's standout performers, winning four consecutive unanimous 5-0 verdicts to storm into the bantamweight final before settling for silver against Australia's Jye Dixon. His medal also formed part of India's historic boxing campaign, which yielded seven golds and three silvers, making the country the No. 1 boxing nation at the Games for the first time.Yet, behind that success lay months of uncertainty, selection hurdles and a weight-category gamble that nearly cost him a place on the flight to Scotland.Speaking exclusively to TimesofIndia.com, former world champion and Jadumani's mentor, Laishram Sarita Devi, recounted how the young boxer refused to abandon his Olympic dream even when every obstacle seemed stacked against him.Jadumani had built his reputation in the 50kg category, winning medals at World Boxing Cups before learning that the division would no longer feature in the Commonwealth Games, Asian Games or Olympic programme.Rather than remain in a non-Olympic category, he decided to move up to 55kg — a division already occupied by some of India's biggest names."He continued to consult with me. Whenever he had to make a big decision, he called up and consulted with me — like increasing his weight category," Sarita told TimesofIndia.com."After he won a World Cup medal in 50kg, he got to know that the weight category is no longer in the CWG, Asian Games and Olympics. He wanted to move to 55kg."The decision immediately brought fresh challenges."Army had their No. 1 boxer in the 55kg category in Pune, who is Services' No. 1 boxer. And the weight category also has Amit Panghal — Olympian and Asian champion. He said he wanted to move up the weight to compete at CWG, Asian Games etc, but was discouraged by hearing questions like whether he would be able to compete at that level, which created a doubt in him," she said.Sarita, however, wanted only one answer: "We sat down and I asked him, 'Are you confident about the decision?' He said he was, so I told him to move up the category."The decision created another problem.Without competing in the National Championships, Jadumani could not enter the national coaching camp. But because he belonged to the Army Sports Institute, Services already had its designated 55kg representative. Attempts to let him represent Manipur also failed."We tried to make him compete for the state of Manipur, but we didn't get an NOC because he is with the Army," Sarita said.Relief finally arrived through a Boxing Federation of India (BFI) policy that granted direct entries to the National Championships for World Boxing Cup medallists. The move was aimed at rewarding elite international performers and ensuring they were not blocked by the usual domestic qualification pathways.The decision allowed Jadumani to compete directly in the 55kg draw despite the institutional overlap, resulting in multiple squad members — Pawan Bartwal, Jadumani Singh and Amit Panghal — finding themselves in the same weight-category draw.Sarita said her ward grabbed the opportunity with both hands."He then got a chance to compete in 55kg in the Nationals. Due to his effort, he won against the Services No.1, Olympians etc to be named Best Boxer in the Nationals. After that he got the chance to be part of the India camp," she said.He then cleared the final selection trials, which included physical assessments alongside ring performances."He participated in the final trial for the CWG and Asian Games — which had many aspects like strength and endurance tests before fighting in the ring. He won all of it to get selected for the CWG and was really happy and started training hard," she added.Just when Glasgow appeared certain, another setback emerged.Because Jadumani had only recently moved into 55kg, he did not possess the Asian ranking required under the Sports Ministry's eligibility criteria for Commonwealth Games selection."He got an explanation mail from the Sports Ministry, which put him in immense tension ahead of the Games," Sarita recalled.Under the ministry's guidelines, boxers were expected to be ranked among Asia's top eight in their respective categories."He was ranked No. 2 in 50kg, but he lacked a ranking in the new 55kg category. He had only competed in one Asian Championship in the new weight category before the trials for CWG and, being new to the category, lost in the quarterfinals," she said.That led to fresh doubts over his selection."He was disheartened when questions were raised whether he was a medal prospect because he was not in the rankings prescribed by the ministry. He called me and said the coaches were saying he may or may not be on the flight to the CWG because of this letter from the ministry," she recalled.The uncertainty only ended after BFI submitted a detailed explanation to the ministry, outlining Jadumani's circumstances following his weight-category switch."BFI replied to the ministry properly, explaining everything and after a lot of effort his ticket to Glasgow was approved. What I like about him is that he is the kind of person who doesn't give up and has a very strong will power," she said.Jadumani eventually reached the final after four demanding contests, each won by an identical 5-0 margin. But Sarita believes the scheduling ultimately worked against him."Jadumani's four bouts were very tough. He played all out in all the bouts till the semifinals as he got proper rest and recovery time. Since the gold medal opponent got a bye earlier, he had fewer bouts than Jadumani," she explained.The semifinal-final turnaround, she felt, proved decisive. There was a one-day gap after every bout until the semifinals, but there was no gap between the semifinal and final in Glasgow."Jadumani fought his semifinal in the evening and got the final bout the next morning only, so he did not get much time for recovery. If it was in the evening, he could have fought better. When he entered the ring for the final, I saw his face and body language sitting here and realised he had not had enough recovery," she said.The experience, she believes, underlines the growing importance of sports science."In such situations, we should look for how we can enhance or speed up the recovery process through sports science. We should discuss it to make sure our boxers can give 100 per cent every time they enter the ring," she added.Sarita first noticed Jadumani as a youngster competing in a local tournament."When I saw Jadumani for the first time, it was a tournament for young boys. His movement was really pleasing and I thought he could become a good boxer in the future. I identified him at that time only and gave him Rs 500 because I was very pleased with his performance," she recalled."Jadumani did not start with me from the grassroots. He learnt his basics from another academy. He came to my academy when he was preparing to enrol in the Army Sports Institute in Pune. At that time, I did not have any infrastructure and was coaching from a makeshift setup. And then Covid happened, we had to train in a very isolated small makeshift place,” she added.Years later, after training together through difficult Covid-19 conditions and watching him overcome one hurdle after another, Sarita believes Glasgow is only the beginning."We missed gold at the CWG, but we will work hard to get gold at the Asian Games for sure," she said.The bigger ambition, however, stretches far beyond continental success."His first and primary target remains Olympic gold. Commonwealth Games and Asian Games are the stepping stones in that journey. He will try to win India's first Olympic gold medal in boxing," Sarita concluded.
Article Summary: Jadumani Singh Mandengbam won silver at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. The 22-year-old Manipuri boxer won four consecutive unanimous 5-0 verdicts to storm into the bantamweight final before settling for silver against Australia's Jye Dixon. His medal also formed part of India's historic boxing campaign, which yielded seven golds and three silvers, making the country the No. 1 boxing nation at the Games.

Article Title: Days after historic CWG gold, Dilip Gavit leaves without meeting Raj Thackeray after two-hour wait

Invited, but left waiting

A champion who made history in Glasgow

A journey built on resilience

Just days after scripting history for Indian para athletics at the Commonwealth Games, gold medallist Dilip Gavit found himself making headlines for a very different reason. The 23-year-old sprinter, who became India's first-ever Commonwealth Games gold medallist in the men's 100m T47 event, waited for nearly two hours to meet Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray in Nashik on Thursday before leaving without the meeting taking place.According to Gavit's coach quoted by PTI, Vaijanath Kale, the para-athlete had been invited to meet Thackeray during the MNS chief's visit to Nashik. However, despite arriving at the scheduled venue, Gavit and his coach were made to wait for nearly two hours. A video from the venue showed MNS workers requesting the duo to wait longer while trying to explain that Thackeray was occupied."We were waiting for quite some time... Sir is busy. We will meet him later," Kale is heard saying in the video before they eventually left.The incident came just days after Gavit delivered one of India's biggest moments at the Commonwealth Games. Clocking a Games-record 10.71 seconds, the Nashik sprinter won the men's 100m T47 gold medal, leading a historic Indian one-two finish alongside Mohammed Basil Morssinganakath, who claimed silver. The victory marked India's first-ever Commonwealth Games gold medal in para athletics 100m T47.Gavit's success carries a deeper significance given his remarkable journey. Born into an economically disadvantaged tribal family in Maharashtra, he lost his right arm in a childhood accident. His life changed when coach Vaijanath Kale took him under his wing at the age of 12, supporting his education and athletic development. After winning gold in Glasgow, Gavit emotionally dedicated the medal to Kale, crediting his coach for transforming his life.
Article Summary: Dilip Gavit was invited to meet Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray. The 23-year-old sprinter waited for nearly two hours for the meeting to take place.
